entries.title: Neolithic Anatolian obsidian reaches Central Europe (~2,200 km)
entries.dateMeaning: Trace-element XRF provenance of Neolithic obsidian blades excavated in southern Poland
entries.place: Nemrut Dağ source to southern Poland
entries.summary: Three Neolithic obsidian blades recovered in Poland match eastern Anatolian Nemrut Dağ geochemistry, documenting relay conveyance across roughly 2,200 km from eastern Turkey into central Europe.
entries.detail: Hughes et al. (2025) chemically separated rare eastern Anatolian blades from dominant Carpathian obsidian assemblages in Neolithic Central Europe.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic endpoint link between geological source and Polish findspot; intermediate relay stages remain reconstructed.

entries.title: Neolithic Alpine jadeitite axes reach northwestern Iberia
entries.dateMeaning: Petrographic and FTIR sourcing of prestige stone axes and early amber in Iberia
entries.place: Monte Viso / Western Alps to Galicia & Iberia
entries.summary: Alpine high-pressure jadeitite axes (reaching Vilapedre in Galicia) and pre-Bell Beaker Baltic amber arrivals in northeastern Iberia attest long-distance Neolithic exchange across Western Europe.
entries.detail: Lantes Suárez et al. (2021) provenance Galician jade prestige axes to Western Alpine sources, while Murillo-Barroso et al. (2023) document early Baltic amber arrivals in Western Europe.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic western corridor bridging river valleys and Atlantic coastal conveyance.

entries.title: Alpine & Carpathian copper feeds Nordic Bronze Age Scandinavia
entries.dateMeaning: Lead-isotope and trace-element provenancing of Scandinavian and Dutch bronzes
entries.summary: Nordic Bronze Age metallurgy relied on shifting supplies of Balkan, Slovakian, and Italian Alpine copper channeled northward through Central Europe and the Low Countries in exchange for Baltic amber.
entries.detail: Nørgaard et al. (2021), Vandkilde et al. (2024), and Merkel et al. (2026) correlate major Nordic and Dutch bronze phases with Alpine and Carpathian copper supply shifts.
entries.uncertainty: Commingled recycled alloys obscure direct single-route trajectories across continental river systems.

entries.title: Baltic-to-Adriatic & Central Balkan Bronze Age amber and metal corridor
entries.dateMeaning: Spectroscopic amber sourcing across Central Europe, Carpathian Basin, Balkans, and Adriatic
entries.place: Gdańsk / Baltic Coast to Carpathians, Serbia/Bosnia & Adriatic
entries.summary: Succinite Baltic amber moved southward through Tumulus and Carpathian Basin communities into Serbia, Bosnia, and the Adriatic coast alongside raw copper and bronze circulation.
entries.detail: Cwaliński (2024, 2025) traces the shifting social role and route density of Baltic amber connecting northern basins with the Central Balkans and Adriatic.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic endpoint connection spanning Poland, Slovakia, the Danube, and Sava-Drina valleys.

entries.title: Cornish tin enters Atlantic-to-Sardinian Bronze Age metal circuits
entries.dateMeaning: Tin, lead, and osmium isotope systematics on Late Bronze Age ingots and Nuragic metalwork
entries.place: Cornwall, southwest Britain to Nuragic Sardinia
entries.summary: Isotopic signatures from Late Bronze Age tin ingots match British/Cornish tin, linked through Atlantic seaways to Nuragic Sardinia’s international metal entrepôts.
entries.detail: Williams et al. (2025), Berger et al. (2019), and Sabatini et al. (2026) place Cornwall and Sardinia on intersecting Atlantic–Mediterranean metal supply chains.
entries.uncertainty: Atlantic-to-Mediterranean cargoes likely switched vessels across coastal emporia rather than sailing nonstop under one crew.

entries.title: Sardinia-to-Crete Late Bronze Age tin and oxhide copper circulation
entries.dateMeaning: Tin and lead isotope systematics on Mochlos (Crete) ingots and Sardinian assemblages
entries.summary: Nuragic Sardinian maritime hubs linked central Mediterranean metal traffic with Minoan–Mycenaean Crete (Mochlos) and Cypriot–Levantine oxhide ingot networks.
entries.detail: Berger et al. (2019) and Sabatini et al. (2026) connect Sardinian maritime activity with eastern Mediterranean tin ingot chemistry.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic sea link across the central-eastern Mediterranean; multiple island ports mediated shipping.

entries.title: Phoenician & Punic glass bead and Baltic amber exchange to southern Iberia
entries.dateMeaning: Natron glass archaeometry (Vinha das Caliças 4), Punic amphorae, and amber IR analyses
entries.place: Carthage to Vinha das Caliças (southern Portugal)
entries.summary: Phoenician-Punic maritime lanes carried primary natron glass beads, central Mediterranean amphorae, and Baltic amber (replacing Sicilian simetite) via Qart-Hadasht/Cartagena to southern Portugal.
entries.detail: Lončarić et al. (2024), Victoria et al. (2024), and Murillo-Barroso et al. (2018) combine glass archaeometry, ceramic petrography, and amber analyses across Iron Age Iberia.
entries.uncertainty: Combines Early Iron Age Phoenician foundation phases with late 3rd-century BCE Punic wartime logistics.
entries.destinationName: Vinha das Caliças 4, Beja, southern Portugal

entries.title: Trans-Alpine & Central European Iron Age amber and metal network
entries.dateMeaning: Alpine archaeozoology, amber workshops, and lead-isotope metal provenancing
entries.place: Stufles / Po-Alpine passes to Chełmno & Moravia
entries.summary: Early Iron Age and La Tène amber workshops in Moravia/Central Europe mediated exchange linking Mediterranean Italian–Etruscan markets through Alpine passes (Stufles) to copper and amber hubs in Poland.
entries.detail: Eccher et al. (2025), Dulęba (2023), Golec Mírová et al. (2026), and Kowalski et al. (2026) document synchronized north-south movement of worked amber, Mediterranean copper/lead, and prestige livestock across Central Europe.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic axis connecting trans-Alpine passes with Central European amber and metal workshops.

entries.title: Roman Aquileia–Noricum–Pannonia Imperial Amber Road
entries.dateMeaning: Epigraphic prosopography of Aquileian merchant families and Po Valley ceramic trade
entries.place: Aquileia & Po Valley north to Carnuntum & Baltic
entries.summary: North Italic families from Aquileia — linked with Po River commercial networks — established trading communities through Emona, Noricum, and Pannonia (Balaton and Carnuntum) channeling Baltic raw amber into the Roman Empire.
entries.detail: Gregoratti (2021) traces Aquileian merchant epigraphy along the northern tract of the Roman Amber Road, while Ardis (2023) demonstrates the Po River artery feeding Regio X and trans-Alpine distribution.
entries.uncertainty: Imperial merchant settlement continued into the 2nd–3rd centuries CE; shown through the 100 CE focus period.
